stageDescription: Named external standards and regulators: what each addresses and when to reach for it.
title: ISO/IEC 42001

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable international standard for an AI Management System (AIMS): the policies, roles, processes and checks an organisation uses to govern AI responsibly, and to prove it to an independent auditor.

## Explained like you're 10

Think about a restaurant's food hygiene certificate.

It isn't a recipe for one dish. It's about **how the whole kitchen is run**: who's in charge of safety, the rules everyone follows, fridge temperatures checked and written down every day, staff trained, problems fixed and recorded. Then an inspector visits to check it's really happening, not just written on a poster. They come back every year.

ISO 42001 is that certificate for how a company handles AI. It doesn't say "build your chatbot this way". It says: have an AI policy, know every AI system you use, decide who's responsible, check the risks and the effects on people, keep records, watch the systems, fix problems, and get better every year. An auditor checks the evidence.

The key idea: **it certifies the organisation's system for governing AI, not any single AI product.**

## Why it exists, and why companies want it

Published in December 2023, it was the world's first certifiable AI management system standard. Before it, "we use AI responsibly" was a claim nobody could independently check. 42001 made it auditable, the same way ISO/IEC 27001 did for information security.

It uses the **Harmonized Structure** shared by ISO 27001, ISO 9001 and other management system standards: the same clause numbers and the same Plan-Do-Check-Act logic. A company already certified to 27001 can bolt 42001 onto existing machinery such as internal audit, document control and management review.

| Why a company pursues it | What it gets |
| --- | --- |
| Customer and procurement pressure | Answering "how do you govern AI?" with a certificate instead of a 50-page questionnaire |
| Regulatory readiness | A management backbone that supports EU AI Act duties, especially the quality management system for high-risk AI |
| Internal discipline | One consistent way of approving, monitoring and improving every AI system |
| Market signal | Cloud providers and AI vendors began certifying in 2024-2025, and buyers started asking suppliers for it |

**For you as a consultant:** most 42001 work is gap assessments, building the AIMS, writing policies and the Statement of Applicability, and certification readiness. The JD you prepared for listed "ISO/IEC 42001 Lead Implementer or Lead Auditor" as a preferred credential.

## Level 1: Key words

| Term | Plain meaning | Like you're 10 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Management system | The set of policies, roles, processes and records that make something happen consistently | The way the kitchen is run, not one meal |
| AIMS | AI Management System: a management system for governing AI | The kitchen's rules, specifically for AI |
| Scope | Which parts of the organisation and which AI systems the AIMS covers | Which kitchens the inspector checks |
| Interested parties | Anyone who affects or is affected by the AI: customers, staff, regulators, suppliers | Diners, cooks, the health inspector, the food supplier |
| Documented information | Records and documents the standard requires you to keep | The fridge-temperature logbook |
| AI objectives | Measurable goals for responsible AI | "Zero food poisoning complaints this year" |
| Nonconformity | Something not meeting a requirement | A fridge found too warm |
| Corrective action | Fixing the cause so it doesn't happen again | Repairing the fridge and adding a daily check |
| Statement of Applicability (SoA) | A list of all 38 Annex A controls stating which apply, why, and whether they're in place | The inspector's checklist, filled in by you, with reasons |
| PDCA | Plan, Do, Check, Act: the improvement cycle the clauses follow | Plan the menu, cook, taste, adjust the recipe |

### Your organisation's role

Clause 4 asks the organisation to decide its **role** for each AI system, because duties differ by role:

- **AI provider:** offers an AI product, platform or rervice.
- **AI producer:** designs, develops, tests or deploys AI.
- **AI customer:** uses an AI system, including as a user.
- **AI partner:** for example a system integrator or data supplier.
- **AI subject:** someone affected by the AI, such as a person whose data is used.

A bank is usually an **AI customer** for vendor tools and an **AI producer** for models it builds itself. The same organisation can hold several roles. This matters because some Annex A controls, especially the data controls in A.7, bite mainly on producers.

[embedded content: ISO 42001 clauses on the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle\]

If you forget a clause number in an interview, rebuild it from this loop: plan it, do it, check it, fix it.

## Level 2: Clauses 4-10

Clauses 1-3 are scope, references and definitions. **Clauses 4-10 are the requirements an auditor checks.** Every one is mandatory; you can't exclude a clause, only Annex A controls.

| Clause | Sub-clauses | What it requires | What the auditor wants to see |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 Context | 4.1 organisation and context (incl. your AI roles); 4.2 interested parties; 4.3 scope; 4.4 the AIMS | Understand your situation and draw the boundary | Context analysis, stakeholder list, scope statement, AI system register |
| 5 Leadership | 5.1 commitment; 5.2 AI policy; 5.3 roles, responsibilities, authorities | Top management owns it, visibly | Signed AI policy, RACI, evidence leaders are involved |
| 6 Planning | 6.1.1 general; **6.1.2 AI risk assessment; 6.1.3 AI risk treatment (incl. SoA); 6.1.4 AI system impact assessment**; 6.2 AI objectives; 6.3 planning changes | Decide how you'll find and treat risks and impacts, and what you're aiming for | Risk and impact methods, SoA, risk treatment plan, measurable objectives |
| 7 Support | 7.1 resources; 7.2 competence; 7.3 awareness; 7.4 communication; 7.5 documented information | People, skills and records to run it | Training records, communication plan, document control |
| 8 Operation | 8.1 operational planning and control; **8.2 risk assessment; 8.3 risk treatment; 8.4 impact assessment** (actually performed) | Do what Clause 6 planned, for every system, at planned intervals and on significant change | Completed assessments per system, lifecycle controls running |
| 9 Performance evaluation | 9.1 monitoring and measurement; 9.2 internal audit; 9.3 management review | Check it works | KPIs, internal audit report, management review minutes |
| 10 Improvement | 10.1 continual improvement; 10.2 nonconformity and corrective action | Fix problems at the root and keep improving | Nonconformity log, corrective action records |

**The pattern to remember:** Clause 6 sets up the *method*; Clause 8 *runs* it. Risk assessment, risk treatment and impact assessment each appear twice (6.1.2-6.1.4 and 8.2-8.4) for exactly that reason. Interviewers like this point.

## Level 3: Annex A, the 38 controls

Annex A is a menu of controls grouped under 9 objectives (A.2 to A.10). You must **consider** every one, then include it or justify excluding it in the Statement of Applicability. Numbering tip: the ".1" in each group is the objective, so controls start at ".2".

Like you're 10: Annex A is the full list of kitchen safety rules. A café that never cooks meat can skip the meat-thermometer rule, but it has to write down why.

| Objective | Controls | In plain words |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A.2 Policies related to AI (3) | A.2.2 AI policy; A.2.3 alignment with other policies; A.2.4 review of the AI policy | Have an AI policy, link it to HR, procurement and security policies, and review it |
| A.3 Internal organisation (2) | A.3.2 AI roles and responsibilities; A.3.3 reporting of concerns | Who does what, and a safe way to raise concerns |
| A.4 Resources for AI systems (5) | A.4.2 resource documentation; A.4.3 data resources; A.4.4 tooling resources; A.4.5 system and computing resources; A.4.6 human resources | Know and document the data, tools, compute and skills each system needs |
| A.5 Assessing impacts of AI systems (4) | A.5.2 impact assessment process; A.5.3 documentation of impact assessments; A.5.4 impact on individuals or groups; A.5.5 societal impacts | Assess and record effects on people and society |
| A.6 AI system life cycle (9) | A.6.1.2 objectives for responsible development; A.6.1.3 processes for responsible design and development; A.6.2.2 requirements and specification; A.6.2.3 design and development documentation; A.6.2.4 verification and validation; A.6.2.5 deployment; A.6.2.6 operation and monitoring; A.6.2.7 technical documentation; A.6.2.8 event logs | Control each stage from design to monitoring, with documents and logs |
| A.7 Data for AI systems (5) | A.7.2 data for development and enhancement; A.7.3 acquisition of data; A.7.4 quality of data; A.7.5 data provenance; A.7.6 data preparation | Data is lawful, good quality, traceable and properly prepared |
| A.8 Information for interested parties (4) | A.8.2 system documentation and information for users; A.8.3 external reporting; A.8.4 communication of incidents; A.8.5 information for interested parties | Tell users and others what they need to know, including about incidents |
| A.9 Use of AI systems (3) | A.9.2 processes for responsible use; A.9.3 objectives for responsible use; A.9.4 intended use | Use AI only as intended, with human oversight |
| A.10 Third-party and customer relationships (3) | A.10.2 allocating responsibilities; A.10.3 suppliers; A.10.4 customers | Split responsibilities with vendors and customers, and manage AI suppliers |

Total: 3 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 9 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 3 = **38**.

**The controls interviewers name most:** A.5 (impact assessment), A.6.2.6 (monitoring), A.9.2 (human oversight in use), A.10.3 (suppliers), A.7.4 (data quality).

### The other annexes

| Annex | What it is | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B | Implementation guidance for each Annex A control | How to actually build each control |
| C | Possible AI objectives (such as fairness, privacy, robustness, transparency) and risk sources (such as level of automation, lack of explainability, ML-specific issues) | A starting point for your risk taxonomy and objectives |
| D | Using the AIMS across domains and sectors | Fitting it into sector rules such as banking or health |

**Annex A isn't the limit.** If your risk assessment finds a risk Annex A doesn't cover, you add your own control. Annex A is a checklist to make sure nothing obvious is missed, not the whole answer.

## Level 4: Risk assessment, impact assessment, treatment and the SoA

This is the engine of the standard and the part interviewers probe hardest.

|  | AI risk assessment (6.1.2, 8.2) | AI system impact assessment (6.1.4, 8.4) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asks | What could stop us meeting our AI objectives, and how likely and serious is it? | What could this system do to people and society? |
| Looks at | Risks to the organisation (which includes harm to others) | Consequences for individuals, groups and society |
| Output | Risk register with ratings | Impact assessment record per system |
| Guidance standard | ISO/IEC 23894 | ISO/IEC 42005 (2025) |

Like you're 10: before a school trip, the **risk assessment** asks "what could go wrong for the school?" (lost child, bad publicity, cost). The **impact assessment** asks "how could this trip affect each child?" (the child who can't swim, the child who gets travel sick). You need both, and the second one feeds the first.

### How they connect: the flow

1. **Impact assessment** (6.1.4) identifies effects on people for each AI system.
2. **Risk assessment** (6.1.2) identifies, analyses and rates risks, using the impact results.
3. **Risk treatment** (6.1.3) chooses an option for each risk: modify the system, avoid it, share or transfer it, or accept it.
4. **Choose controls** to deliver the treatment, from Annex A or your own.
5. **Compare with Annex A** to check nothing obvious was missed.
6. **Statement of Applicability:** every Annex A control, included or excluded, with justification and implementation status.
7. **Risk treatment plan:** who does what by when.
8. **Risk owners approve** the plan and accept the residual risk.
9. **Clause 8 repeats it** for each system, at planned intervals and whenever something significant changes.

### What a Statement of Applicability row looks like

| Control | Applicable? | Justification | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A.6.2.6 Operation and monitoring | Yes | GenAI systems can drift or hallucinate in production; monitoring needed to meet AI objective 2 | Implemented: weekly groundedness sample, KRI dashboard |
| A.7.3 Acquisition of data | No | The organisation does not train models; it uses vendor models with RAG over internal documents. Document governance is covered by an internal control (KB-01) | Not applicable |

The second row shows a mature move: excluding a control with a reason, then covering the real risk with your own control. Auditors respect that more than ticking everything "yes".
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick an AI system you know (Help Hub, or any other). Write its scope statement (one sentence: what's in, what's excluded and why), then write 2 rows of a Statement of Applicability for it (one 'Yes, applicable' row and one 'No, excluded' row), following the format in the examples above.

stops.title: Level 5: Certification and how it fits
stops.contentMd:
## Level 5: Certification and how it fits

### The certification path

1. **Gap assessment** against clauses 4-10 and Annex A.
2. **Build the AIMS:** scope, policy, roles, risk and impact methods, SoA, controls.
3. **Run it long enough to create evidence:** scompleted assessments, monitoring results, at least one internal audit (9.2) and one management review (9.3).
4. **Stage 1 audit:** the certification body checks documents and readiness.
5. **Stage 2 audit:** it checks the system actually works: interviews, samples, records.
6. **Certificate** valid for 3 years, with **surveillance audits every year** and recertification at year 3.

Auditors raise **major nonconformities** (a requirement not met at all, blocking certification until fixed) and **minor nonconformities** (partial gaps, fixed within an agreed time). Certification bodies are themselves accredited, and [ISO/IEC 42006:2025](https://www.iso.org/standard/42006) sets the rules for bodies certifying AI management systems.

The two credentials in the JD: a **Lead Implementer** builds an AIMS; a **Lead Auditor** audits one.

### How it fits with other frameworks

| Compared with | Relationship |
| --- | --- |
| ISO/IEC 27001 | Same structure. Reuse internal audit, document control, management review and supplier processes; add the AI-specific parts (roles, impact assessment, Annex A) |
| NIST AI RMF | NIST is a good risk method to run inside clauses 6 and 8; NIST publishes a crosswalk between the two |
| EU AI Act | 42001 supports the Act's quality management system (Art 17) and risk management (Art 9), but certification is **not** EU AI Act compliance. European standards bodies are writing separate standards for the Act |
| ISO/IEC 23894 and 42005 | Guidance on how to do the risk assessment and the impact assessment that 42001 requires |

### Limits and criticisms

- **It certifies the system, not outcomes.** A certified organisation can still deploy a biased model; the certificate shows it has a process to catch and fix that.
- **Scope can be narrow.** A company can certify one product line. Always ask: "what's in scope?"
- **Paper compliance risk.** Documents can look perfect while practice lags. Stage 2 and surveillance audits exist to catch that, through sampling and interviews.

## Worked implementation: Barclays frontline AI inside an AIMS

**This is hypothetical.** It shows how Barclays UK Consumer Banking and Lending Operations *could have* run your three AI projects inside an ISO 42001 AIMS. It doesn't claim Barclays did this. Use it in an interview as: "If I were implementing 42001 there, this is how it would work." Every sample artefact below is short on purpose, to show the shape.

### Step 1: Context and scope (Clause 4)

- **External issues:** FCA Consumer Duty, DISP complaint rules, FCA guidance on vulnerable customers, UK GDPR, PRA model risk expectations, fast GenAI adoption.
- **Interested parties:** customers (including vulnerable ones), contact-centre agents, the FCA and ICO, AI vendors (speech-to-text and LLM providers), internal audit.
- **Roles:** AI customer for vendor models; AI producer for the RAG configuration, NLP thresholds and the AVM integration.
- **Scope statement (sample):** "The AIMS covers AI systems used in Consumer Banking and Lending Operations to support customer interactions: the Help Hub RAG assistant, call summarisation with complaint and vulnerability detection, and the mortgage rate selector's automated valuation model. The COI automation is excluded because it contains no AI."

### Step 2: Leadership (Clause 5)

- **AI policy (sample statements):** AI outputs that reach customers are grounded in approved sources and checked by a trained person. Every AI system has one accountable owner. Thresholds that decide customer outcomes are risk-appetite decisions owned by Risk, not engineering defaults.
- **RACI:** accountable executive for the AIMS; a named owner per system; the 1LOD controls team assesses and tests controls; 2LOD Risk and Compliance challenges; internal audit gives assurance.

### Step 3: AI objectives (Clause 6.2)

Measurable, and each with an owner:

1. 100% of in-scope systems have a current impact assessment.
2. Help Hub knowledge base updated within 48 hours of any policy change.
3. Source-verification rate on regulated Help Hub queries of at least 80%.
4. Complaint-detection recall at or above the level Risk has approved.
5. Every mortgage customer can see the valuation and balance used to decide their deals.

### Step 4: Impact assessments (Clasuses 6.1.4, 8.4)

| System | Who is affected | Possible impact | Severity | Reversible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Help Hub | Customers advised by agents | Wrong norng lending or rights information leads to a poor decision or complaint | Medium-high | Partly |
| Vulnerability detection | Vulnerable customers | Vulnerability missed, so no support offered | High | Hard |
| Complaint detection | Dissatisfied customers | Complaint not recorded or handled under DISP | High | Partly |
| Speech-to-text | Customers with strong accents or non-native English | Poorer transcription, so more missed disclosures | Medium | Partly |
| Mortgage selector (AVM) | Remortgaging customers | Shown worse deals due to an unseen valuation | Medium | Yes, with a query route |

### Step 5: Risk register (Clauses 6.1.2, 8.2), extract

| ID | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Rating | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Help Hub gives ungrounded answers on regulated topics | Medium | High | High | Modify: groundedness testing, low temperature, "I don't know" behaviour |
| R2 | Outdated or draft policy retrieved | High | High | High | Modify: document owners, approval workflow, 48-hour SLA, retire old versions |
| R3 | Agents skip source verification | High | Medium | High | Modify: mandatory logged verification, verification-rate KRI |
| R4 | Complaint threshold tuned for few alerts, missing complaints | Medium | High | High | Modify: Risk owns the threshold, recall target, documented rationale |
| R5 | Retraining on agent ratings teaches the model to under-report | Medium | High | High | Modify: governance gate before ratings enter retraining |
| R6 | Vendor changes model without notice | Low | Medium | Medium | Share: contract clauses, regression tests on version change |

### Step 6: Statement of Applicability, extract (Clause 6.1.3)

| Control | Applicable? | How it's met here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A.3.2 Roles and responsibilities | Yes | Owners named for each system, knowledge base and threshold |
| A.5.4 Impact on individuals or groups | Yes | Step 4, with a vulnerable-customer focus |
| A.6.2.4 Verification and validation | Yes | Groundedness test set; speech-to-text accuracy tested across accents |
| A.6.2.5 Deployment | Yes | Release gate requires impact assessment and 2LOD sign-off |
| A.6.2.6 Operation and monitoring | Yes | KRI dashboard: knowledge-base lag, verification rate, escalation rate, query failure rate |
| A.6.2.8 Event logs | Yes | Each answer logs question, sources, model version and agent verification |
| A.8.2 Information for users | Yes | LTV breakdown shown to mortgage customers; agent guidance on Help Hub limits |
| A.9.2 Responsible use | Yes | Agents must verify sources before relaying regulated guidance |
| A.10.3 Suppliers | Yes | AI clauses in speech-to-text and LLM vendor contracts |
| A.7.3 Acquisition of data | No | No model training in scope; document governance covered by internal control KB-01 |

### Step 7: Support (Clause 7)

Training for agents on what Help Hub can and can't do and why verification matters; competence records for the controls team; a communication plan for telling customers about call analytics; document control for the policy library feeding Help Hub.

### Step 8: Operation (Clasuse 8)

Every change, including a new policy set in the knowledge base, a vendor model version or a retraining cycle, triggers a light re-assessment. KRIs run monthly and feed the risk register. Vendor performance is reviewed quarterly.

### Step 9: Performance evaluation (Clause 9)

- **Internal audit finding (sample):** "3 of 20 sampled knowledge-base documents were past their review date. Minor nonconformity against A.6.2.6 and the 48-hour objective."
- **Management review agenda:** objective status, KRI trends, incidents, audit findings, vendor issues, regulatory changes, resources.

### Step 10: Improvement (Clause 10)

- **Corrective action (sample):** root cause: no named owner for 40% of documents. Fix: owners assigned, automatic expiry alerts. Effectiveness check: re-sample after 3 months.

### The interview line

"My Help Hub findings would have been nonconformities under 42001: the optional verification against A.9.2, the knowledge-base gap against A.6.2.6 and A.3.2. Under an AIMS, each would go through Clause 10 corrective action with a root cause and an effectiveness check, instead of sitting in a findings log."
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick a system you've actually worked with. Write your own 10-step worked implementation sketch (one short bullet per step, matching the Barclays structure above: context/scope, leadership, objectives, impact assessment, risk register, SoA extract, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement). It can be brief, but every step needs at least one concrete detail.

stops.title: Applied to your CV: the control to cite for each finding
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV: the control to cite for each finding

Your CV says you're studying ISO 42001. When an interviewer tests that, citing the right Annex A control for each finding proves it in one sentence.

| Your finding | Annex A control | Clause link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Help Hub source verification optional | A.9.2 Processes for responsible use (human oversight) | 8.1 |
| Help Hub knowledge base had no owner or SLA | A.3.2 Roles and responsibilities; A.6.2.6 Operation and monitoring | 5.3, 9.1 |
| Drafts and old versions retrievable | A.6.2.6 Operation and monitoring; own control for document governance | 6.1.3 |
| Hallucination testing on regulated queries | A.6.2.4 Verification and validation | 8.1 |
| Mortgage selector hid the AVM valuation | A.8.2 System documentation and information for users | 7.4 |
| Speech-to-text untested across accents | A.6.2.4 Verification and validation; A.5.4 Impact on individuals or groups | 6.1.4 |
| Complaint threshold set by engineering | A.3.2 Roles and responsibilities | 6.1.3 (risk owner accepts residual risk) |
| Feedback loop retraining unchecked | A.6.2.5 Deployment (change control); A.7.4 Quality of data | 6.3, 8.1 |
| Vulnerability triggers without safeguarding input | A.5.4 Impact on individuals or groups | 6.1.4 |
| Speech-to-text and LLM vendors | A.10.3 Suppliers; A.10.2 Allocating responsibilities | 8.1 |
| KRIs you designed | A.6.2.6 Operation and monitoring | 9.1 |

**Honesty check:** say "I'm studying 42001" and "if this had been run under 42001". Don't imply Barclays was certified or that you implemented an AIMS.

## Free videos and courses

Free only. The standard itself is sold by ISO and national bodies; there is no free full copy, but ISO's site shows a preview. Suggested path: 1, then 2, then the podcast episodes in 4, then 3 for an auditor's view. Claude could not play the videos directly; details come from host and listing pages.

### Videos and webinars

| # | Resource | Source | Length | Level | Why watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [What is ISO/IEC 42001? Quick Guide to AIMS](https://vimeo.com/1064244737) | Links to the ISO website; uploader not confirmed | \~8+ min | Beginner | What an AIMS is, who it's for, benefits |
| 2 | [ISO 42001 structure and AIMS scope explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X_tICMwOlgE) | InfosecTrain (training company) | 18 min | Beginner | Walks the clause structure and scope |
| 3 | [Responsible AI for regulated industries: applying ISO 42001](https://www.dqsglobal.com/en/learn/webinar-recordings/responsible-ai-for-regulated-industries-applying-iso-42001) | DQS, a certification body | 1.5 hrs | Core | Free, but you register with your email. Requirements, tools and case studies from people who certify |

### Audio

| # | Resource | Length | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | [The ISO Review Podcast: ISO/IEC 42001 clauses 4-7](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1986613/episodes/15753623-iso-iec-42001-ai-management-system-standard-clauses-4-7) (Sep 2024), plus the same show's episodes on [clauses 8.1-8.4](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1986613/episodes/15833443-iso-iec-42001-ai-management-system-standard-claWses-8-1-8-4) and [Annexes C and D](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1986613/episodes/17230651-iso-iec-42001-ai-management-system-standard-annex-c-and-annex-d) | \~36 min each | Two management-system auditors read through the clauses. Good for a commute |

Left out: LRQA's one-day ISO 42001 introduction is listed as free-certificate but costs about 640 pounds. BSI's launch webinar was a live event with no confirmed recording.
stops.artifactPrompt: Write your own 'finding → Annex A control → clause link' table with at least 3 rows from your own work history, the way the Help Hub table does. Include the honesty-check phrasing: say 'if this had been run under 42001', never that your past employer was certified.

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| What is ISO 42001? | The certifiable international standard for an AI Management System: how an organisation governs AI and proves it to an auditor. Published December 2023. |
| How is it structured? | Clauses 4-10 in the Harmonized Structure (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement), plus Annex A with 38 controls across 9 objectives. |
| Risk assessment vs impact assessment? | Risk assessment (6.1.2) looks at risks to the organisation and its AI objectives. Impact assessment (6.1.4) looks at consequences for individuals, groups and society, and feeds the risk assessment. |
| What is the Statement of Applicability? | A list of all Annex A controls, saying which apply, why, and their status. Exclusions need a justification. |
| Can you exclude a clause? | No. Clauses 4-10 are mandatory; only Annex A controls can be excluded, with justification. |
| Name some Annex A objectives | Policies (A.2), internal organisation (A.3), resources (A.4), impact assessment (A.5), lifecycle (A.6), data (A.7), information for interested parties (A.8), use of AI (A.9), third parties (A.10). |
| Which control covers monitoring? | A.6.2.6, AI system operation and monitoring. Supported by A.6.2.8, event logs. |
| Which control covers human oversight in use? | A.9.2, processes for responsible use. |
| How does certification work? | Gap assessment, build the AIMS, run it with internal audit and management review, Stage 1 (documents), Stage 2 (effectiveness), 3-year certificate with annual surveillance. |
| Does 42001 make you EU AI Act compliant? | No. It supports the quality management system and risk management, but the Act has product-level duties like conformity assessment and CE marking. |
| You have ISO 27001. How hard is 42001? | Easier: same structure, so reuse audit, document control, management review and supplier processes. The new work is AI roles, the impact assessment and the AI-specific controls. |
| What do organisations usually miss? | An incomplete AI inventory (vendor features), impact assessments skipped or done once, no AI clauses in supplier contracts, objectives that aren't measurable, incident processes not extended to AI. |
| Weakness of 42001? | It certifies the process, not the outcomes, and scope can be drawn narrowly. |

quiz.question: What is ISO 42001?
quiz.answer: The certifiable international standard for an AI Management System (AIMS): how an organisation governs AI and proves it to an auditor. Published December 2023.
quiz.explanation: The world's first certifiable AI management system standard — distinct from a product-level or legal standard.

quiz.question: How is ISO 42001 structured?
quiz.answer: Clauses 4-10 in the Harmonized Structure (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement), plus Annex A with 38 controls across 9 objectives.
quiz.explanation: Same structure as ISO 27001 and ISO 9001 — this reuse is exactly why certified organisations find 42001 easier to bolt on.

quiz.question: Risk assessment vs impact assessment — what's the difference?
quiz.answer: Risk assessment (6.1.2) looks at risks to the organisation and its AI objectives. Impact assessment (6.1.4) looks at consequences for individuals, groups and society, and feeds the risk assessment.
quiz.explanation: The impact assessment result is an input to the risk assessment, not a separate parallel exercise.

quiz.question: What is the Statement of Applicability?
quiz.answer: A list of all 38 Annex A controls, stating which apply, why, and their implementation status. Exclusions need a justification.
quiz.explanation: The single most audited document in a 42001 certification — auditors probe excluded controls hardest.

quiz.question: Can you exclude a clause?
quiz.answer: No. Clauses 4-10 are mandatory; only Annex A controls can be excluded, and only with justification.
quiz.explanation: A common point of confusion — clauses and Annex A controls have very different exclusion rules.

quiz.question: Name some Annex A objectives.
quiz.answer: Policies (A.2), internal organisation (A.3), resources (A.4), impact assessment (A.5), lifecycle (A.6), data (A.7), information for interested parties (A.8), use of AI (A.9), third parties (A.10).
quiz.explanation: You don't need every control number — knowing the 9 objective groups is usually enough.

quiz.question: Which control covers monitoring?
quiz.answer: A.6.2.6, AI system operation and monitoring, supported by A.6.2.8, event logs.
quiz.explanation: Pairs naturally with an observability or monitoring question in an interview.

quiz.question: Which control covers human oversight in use?
quiz.answer: A.9.2, processes for responsible use.
quiz.explanation: The control most directly tied to a 'was a human actually checking this' finding.

quiz.question: How does certification work?
quiz.answer: Gap assessment, build the AIMS, run it with internal audit and management review, Stage 1 audit (documents and readiness), Stage 2 audit (does it actually work), then a 3-year certificate with annual surveillance audits.
quiz.explanation: Know the full path — gap assessment and building the AIMS is where most consulting work actually sits.

quiz.question: Does ISO 42001 certification make an organisation EU AI Act compliant?
quiz.answer: No. It supports the Act's quality management system and risk management duties, but the Act has separate product-level duties such as conformity assessment and CE marking.
quiz.explanation: A critical distinction to state unprompted — conflating the two is a common mistake.

quiz.question: An organisation already has ISO 27001. How hard is adding 42001?
quiz.answer: Easier than starting from scratch: same structure, so internal audit, document control, management review and supplier processes can be reused. The new work is AI roles, the impact assessment, and the AI-specific Annex A controls.
quiz.explanation: A strong, specific answer beats a vague 'it should be easier' — name exactly what's reused and what's new.

quiz.question: What do organisations usually miss when implementing 42001?
quiz.answer: An incomplete AI inventory (missing vendor features that are themselves AI), impact assessments skipped or done only once, no AI clauses in supplier contracts, objectives that aren't actually measurable, and incident processes not extended to cover AI.
quiz.explanation: Naming these unprompted signals real implementation experience, not just reading the standard.

quiz.question: What's a core weakness of ISO 42001?
quiz.answer: It certifies the process, not the outcomes — a certified organisation can still deploy a biased model — and scope can be drawn narrowly, so always ask what's actually in scope.
quiz.explanation: Naming limits unprompted is what separates a practitioner answer from a marketing one.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. How many Annex A controls, across how many objectives?
2. Which clause sets up the impact assessment, and which clause runs it?
3. What's the difference between Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits?
4. A bank uses a vendor LLM and never trains models. Which Annex A group might it justifiably exclude parts of?
5. Which control would you cite for your Help Hub verification finding?
6. Name the three things Clause 9 requires.
7. Which standard gives guidance on doing the impact assessment?

**Answers:** (1) 38 controls, 9 objectives. (2) 6.1.4 sets it up; 8.4 runs it. (3) Stage 1 checks documents and readiness; Stage 2 checks the system works in practice. (4) A.7, data for AI systems, for example A.7.3 acquisition of data, with a justification and an own control for document governance. (5) A.9.2, responsible use with human oversight. (6) Monitoring and measurement, internal audit, management review. (7) ISO/IEC 42005.

quiz.question: How many Annex A controls are there, across how many objectives?
quiz.answer: 38 controls, across 9 objectives.
quiz.explanation: Know both numbers cold — they come up constantly in structural questions about the standard.

quiz.question: Which clause sets up the impact assessment, and which clause runs it?
quiz.answer: 6.1.4 sets it up (planning); 8.4 runs it (operation, for every system at planned intervals).
quiz.explanation: Mirrors the risk assessment pattern (6.1.2 plans, 8.2 runs) — the same logic applies to both.

quiz.question: What's the difference between Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits?
quiz.answer: Stage 1 checks documents and readiness. Stage 2 checks that the system actually works in practice, through interviews, samples and records.
quiz.explanation: Stage 2 is where paper compliance gets caught out — documents alone don't pass it.

quiz.question: A bank uses a vendor LLM and never trains models. Which Annex A group might it justifiably exclude parts of?
quiz.answer: A.7, data for AI systems — for example A.7.3 acquisition of data — with a justification and its own control covering document governance instead.
quiz.explanation: A textbook example of a mature exclusion: reasoned, documented, and backed by an alternative control.

quiz.question: Which control would you cite for your Help Hub verification finding?
quiz.answer: A.9.2, processes for responsible use, with human oversight.
quiz.explanation: The direct Annex A citation for 'verification was optional and nobody enforced it'.

quiz.question: Name the three things Clause 9 requires.
quiz.answer: Monitoring and measurement (9.1), internal audit (9.2), and management review (9.3).
quiz.explanation: Clause 9 is how you prove the AIMS actually works, not just that it exists on paper.

quiz.question: Which standard gives guidance on doing the impact assessment?
quiz.explanation: ISO/IEC 23894 is the equivalent guidance standard for the risk assessment side.
